TO: The University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, Finance and Facilities Committee FROM: Marc B.
Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: April 13, 2026 SUBJECT: Action Item: Consideration of Bond Issuance Resolution Purpose of Submittal: This request is to approve a resolution to authorize that URI, through the Rhode Island Health and Educational Building Corporation (RIHEBC), issue up to $42.2M in revenue bonds in fall of 2026, and to refund existing bonds if market conditions are deemed favorable.
The following projects would be supported by the new bonds issued under the university’s Education and General covenant, which means that debt service would be covered by the university’s unrestricted funds: 1.
Utility Infrastructure Upgrade – Phase III (total project cost: $9.2M) 2.
Repaving and Hardscape Improvements (total project cost: $20M) 3.

Facilities Service Sector Upgrade (total project cost: $13M) Points to Consider: All debt issuances by State agencies must receive authorization from the state legislature, called "Kushner authorizations" after Linda Kushner, the representative who sponsored the bill requiring them.
The Kushner authorization for the Facilities Service Sector Upgrade is included in Article 4 of H7123Aaa which established the State budget for fiscal year 2023.
The Kushner authorization for the Utility Infrastructure Phase III is included in Article 4 of H7225, the budget bill which established the State budget for fiscal year 2025.
The Kushner authorization for the Repaving and Hardscape Improvements project is included in the Governor’s Recommended budget for fiscal year 2027 and is under consideration by the General Assembly.
The first project, Facilities Service Sector Upgrade, involves work to enhance and reorganize facilities within the service sector for more efficient and effective operations, including construction of a new Lands and Grounds Building which is currently housed in a former Dairy Barn that is in very poor condition.

The second project, Utility Infrastructure Phase III, is the third of a four anticipated phases of work to upgrade the University’s primary utility systems to replace infrastructure that is nearing its end of life .
Given the age of this infrastructure, the University experiences unplanned outages that effect multiple campus buildings, interrupting the academic and research programs within.
This project will provide a more stable campus environment through the design and construction of upgrades and component replacements to our municipal-level campus utility system.

The third project, Repaving and Hardscaping, will allow URI to repave and reconstruct parking facilities, roadways, and walkways across three campuses of URI, as well as provide improvements to landscape elements.
This project will support replacing parking lost due to the new undergraduate residential buildings currently under construction as well as the extension and paving of Farmhouse Road, a critical enabling project for the Comprehensive Campus Plan.
We anticipate issuing $4.5M of the total project amount in 2026, with the remainder supported by a future bond issuance.
The University’s Series 2016A and 2016B bonds become refundable as of June 2026, and we anticipate refunding these bonds simultaneously with the new issuance - if market conditions are favorable - to reduce the University’s overall debt service on these bonds.
Approval of this resolution does not commit the university to issue these bonds, if market conditions or other factors result in unfavorable conditions to do so.

The University sought and received approval at the February meeting to allow for reimbursement of expenditures related to the Utilities Phase III project before the issuance of debt supporing the projects, so work could begin in the critical summer months of 2026.
The approved reimbursement amount was capped at $6.91M.
Recommendation: I recommend that the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees approve the enclosed Resolution effective April 13, 2026, to authorize the issuance of RIHEBC bonds in support of these three projects and allow for refunding of any refundable bonds to reduce overall debt service.
Supporting Information: See attached Resolution.
Proposed Motion of the Board: To recommend approval of the resolution authorizing t he borrowing in connection with the issuance of Rhode Island Education Building Corporation Higher Education Facility Revenue Bonds for 1) Utility Infrastructure Upgrade – Phase III; 2) Repaving and Hardscape Improvements; 3) Facilities Service Sector Upgrade; as well as the refunding of Series 2016A and 2016B bonds (if market conditions are favorable) as presented in enclosed Resolution.

OVERVIEW OF THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University had its beginning as the State Agricultural School chartered in 1888.
The federal Morrill Act of 1862 provided the framework within which the school became the land-grant institution of the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) and in 1892, the school became the Rhode Island College of Agricultural and Mechanic Arts.
The first class of 17 members was graduated two years later.

In 1909 the name of the College was changed to Rhode Island State College and the program of study was revised and expa nded.
In 1951, the college became known as the University of Rhode Island by act of the State’s General Assembly.
The University of Rhode Island is the State’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed resid ents and leaders.
URI is committed to high -quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and th e Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.

URI’s Strategic Plan, Focus URI 2023-2033, lays out the strategic vision for the University for the next decade, outlining four strategic priorities and the actions the University will take to achieve them: Strategic Priority 1: Broaden the University’s impact through a reinvigorated commitment to its land- and sea-grant missions and the State of Rhode Island Strategic Priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment Strategic Priority 3: Foster an inclusive, people-centered culture Strategic Priority 4: Implement leading-edge administrative and financial systems and practices to power the University of the future

A-3 The University’s main campus in Kingston, RI encompasses approximately 1,400 acres in Kingston, 30 miles south of Providence in the northeastern metropolitan corridor between New York and Boston.
The 165-acre Narragansett Bay Campus (the “Bay Campus”), located six miles to the east overlooking the west passage of the Narragansett Bay, is home to the Graduate School of Oceanography , and the Ocean Engineering Department of the College of Engineering, and the College of Environment and Life Sciences.
In Providence, the University offers degree programs and non -credit courses and workshops in various locations.
In the western section of the State, 20 miles from Kingston, the 2,300 acres of woods, fields, streams and ponds on the W.
Alton Jones Campus are the site of research by various principal investigators.
The University offers degree programs through the doctoral level.
The University had a combined graduate, undergraduate and dual high school enrollment headcount of 14,452 students for the f all 2024 official reporting.
First year applications for fall 2024 were once again at record levels with 25,391 applications.

GOVERNANCE The Board of Governors for Higher Education became the governing body for the University in 1981, until the Board of Education assumed governance in January 2013.
In 2014, the Board of Education created two councils, including the Council on Postsecondary Education (the “Council”) which exercised oversight of the University, Rhode Island College (“RIC”) and the Community College of Rhode Island (“CCRI”).
On February 1, 2020, governance of the University was transferred to the newly constituted Board of Trustees for the University of Rhode Island (the “Board of Trustees” or the “URI Board”), whose purpose is the oversight of the University .
The Board of Education and the Council continue to provide oversight for RIC and CCRI.
The URI Board assumed all the powers and duties with respect to the University formerly assigned to the Board of Education and the Council.
The State continues to oversee State funding of higher education , approve borrowin g and drive education policy.
The University is held to meeting performance measures required by the State.

The new organizational structure for URI did not materially change the funding or financing arrangements of the State's three public higher education institutions , except in that the URI Board of Trustees ha s final approval of tuition and mandatory fee rates .
The new URI Board continues to share responsibility for its portion of previously issued bonds for the State’s colleges, which include debt issued by all three public h igher institutions in the State: URI, Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island .
The enabling legislation creating the Board of Trustees is codified in Rhode Island General Laws Title 16, Chapter 32.
The Trustees were originally appointed with staggered terms to ensure continuity on the Board.
On an annual basis, trustees are considered for appointment and reappointment by the Governor and are confirmed by the State legislature by the end of each legislative session, typically by June.
Three-year terms will again be staggered, as shown by the term expiration dates of those Trustees who have been reappointed to date.

The Faculty Senate was authorized in 1960 by the general faculty to conduct any business assigned to the faculty by law or by the Rhode Island Board of Education/Council on Postsecondary Education and now by the Board of Trustees .
The Graduate Council is the representative body for the graduate faculty and determines the academic policies for graduate study.

URI’s research enterprise supports strategic priorities that include academic excellence, student success, workforce development, and engagement with the State of Rhode Island.
Sponsored research spans a broad range of disciplines, including engineering, h ealth, environmental studies, social sciences, the arts, and ocean and marine sciences.
These activities enhance academic programs and provide structured experiential learning opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, including laboratory and field research, interdisciplinary work, and creative scholarship.

A core component of URI’s research profile is its long standing leadership in ocean science, coastal resilience, and the Blue Economy , which aligns with institutional strategic priorities and statewide economic development goals.
Through its Graduate School of Oceanography, College of the Environment and Life Sciences, College of Engineering and affiliated research centers, URI serves a s a hub for ocean and marine research, workforce training, and technology development.
The University hosts and supports ocean observing systems, marine instrumentation development, underwater systems research, and data analytics that are relevant to environmental monitoring, national security, fisheries, and offshore infrastructure.
These activities position URI as a key acad emic partner for federal agencies, industry, and regional stakeholders engaged in ocean and maritime technologies.
Research funding is derived from a diversified portfolio of federal agencies, state sources, private foundations, and industry sponsors, supporting financial stability and mitigating reliance on any single funding source.

URI’s research enterprise benefits from sustained participation in multi institutional consortia that enhance research capacity and infrastructure.
For example, the University serves as the long standing home institution for the Rhode Island IDeA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence ( RI INBRE), a statewide consortium focused on strengthening biomedical research capacity and expanding student training opportunities across Rhode Island’s public and private institutions of higher education.
URI also serves as the lead and coordinating institution for Rhode Island’s National Science Foundation Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) E CORE program.
The Rhode Island EPSCoR E CORE Inclusive Network for Excellence in Science and Technology (RII NEST) is designed to strengthen research infrastructure and workforce capacity statewide while promoting equitable, use inspired research.
EPSCoR programming supports undergraduate research and training in laboratory and field methods , data analytics, and scientific communication, aligning with the University’s strategic emphasis on talent development and retention.

Consistent with its land grant and sea grant missions, URI conducts federally funded research addressing environmental, coastal, and public health challenges of direct relevance to Rhode Island and the region.
One such initiative is the Sources, Transport, Exposure and Effects of PFAS (STEEP) project, funded by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences.
STEEP research examines environmental pathways and human health impacts of poly and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) while disseminating findings to inform prevention and mitigation strategies.

Special Academic Opportunities Honors Program The University Honors Program provides students the opportunity to take dynamic, interdisciplinary courses and engage in original research alongside faculty who are leaders in their fields in the sciences, business, and humanities.
The program offers motivated students enrichment opportunities through smaller class sizes, individualized advising and mentoring, and participation in a research or creative project working under the guidance of a faculty mentor.
The program also sponsors a colloquium each year that brings together distinguished national and international experts on contemporary topics who share their thoughts and work with students and the wider community.
National Student Exchange Program National Student Exchange (“NSE”) inspires academic enrichment, personal exploration, and student development by facilitating accessible collegiate study away among member colleges and universities throughout the United States, Canada, Guam, Puerto Rico an d U.S Virgin Islands.
With 159 member institutions, students have access to many options.
Some NSE campuses offer unique opportunities beyond traditional classroom learning.

These include internships, research, field study, and/or other experiential learning opportunities.
Affordable payment options as well as many forms of financial aid are available for participants.

A-12 Center for Career and Experiential Education The University of Rhode Island’s Center for Career and Experiential Education (“CCEE”), part of the Kent and Diane Fannon Institute for Student Success , engages undergraduate students and alumni in a personal and professional educational experience, from admission through employment.
The Center values its relationships with local and national employer partners and seeks to find innovative ways to connect students, alumni, faculty, and employers in the career education and development process.
The team of Career Education Specialists (“CES”) offer individual and group professional development sessions and on-line modules for students and alumni.
The topics include self -assessments to discover one’s strengths, job and internship searching, networking and brand development strategies, resume and cover letter development, salary negotiation, interviewing skills, and major to career industry clusters.
The highest impact practice involves engaging in opportunities and courses which include relevant connections between coursework, the community and the workforce.

CCEE offers service learning and internship courses to explore a variety of occupations and gain practical experience through an internship or civic engagement.
The Employer Relations team develops relationships with local and national employers to connect students and alumni with their desired industries.
This is done through the Rhody Alumni Mentoring (“RAM”) program, career and volunteer fairs, networking events, on -campus interviewing, job, internship and volunteer posting, and professional development week.
Rhode Island Inter-institutional Exchange Full-time students matriculated at one of the public institutions of higher education in Rhode Island may enroll for a maximum of eight credits of their full-time schedule per semester for study at one of the other public institutions at no additional expense.
Each institut ion will determine and maintain the integrity of the degree to be awarded.
The University has a robust system of transfer and prior-approved courses, along with articulation agreements with the Community College of Rhode Island and other feeder institutions.

Study Abroad The Office of International Education & National Student Exchange promotes the internationalization of education and building of students’ cross -cultural global skills through educational opportunities in a variety of global environments and institutional linkages.
While international education was curtailed in the spring of academic year 2020 and fall and spring of academic year 2021 due to the pandemic, the University has resumed international education and exchanges beginning in 2022 -2023.
Participation rates in 2025- 2026 are approaching pre-pandemic levels across the study abroad portfolio.
In a normal year the University offers over 140 study abroad options in more than 43 countries worldwide through URI sponsored programs and global affiliations; off-campus credit bearing experiences exist for students in all academic disciplines.
The wide array of learning experiences managed by the office support the institutional objective of expanding the global learning opportunities available to the student body a nd promoting the institutional objective of ensuring that all students are exposed to global perspectives and building global competency skills.

Options beyond traditional classroom learning are available.
These include international internships, research, field study, virtual engagements and other experiential learning opportunities such as ship-based research voyages.
Semester and short-term programs during the Winter J-Term session, Spring Break, and Summer Session programs are available each academic ye ar.
The office also provides comprehensive advising and programming services – from program selection to predeparture preparation and reentry programming – to support student success in all aspects of the education abroad process and context.
In a concerted effort to increase accessibility and affordability, student assistance in securing local and national scholarship awards is provided and developing quality cost-effective study options is given precedence.
Summer Sessions The University provides a full range of undergraduate and graduate course offerings online and offers the opportunity to attend two five-week in-person sessions and a ten-week session.
Courses begin immediately after Commencement and are offered online, during day and evenings.

Winter J-Term Session URI offers a “J-Term”, which is an academic mini-semester over winter session (the approximately three- week period between January 2 and the day before the spring semester begins) that consists of credit-bearing courses that offer new value-added experiences for students not possible during standard semesters and/or allow students to catch up or retake certain courses.
Over 2400 students take part in this mini -term each year.
Military Science and Leadership (Army Reserve Officers’ Training Corps or “Army ROTC”) Military Science and Leadership is one of the nation’s top leadership programs.
Army ROTC is an elective curriculum that students take along with their required college classes.
The program provides students with tools, training, and experience to help the m succeed in any competitive environment.
Army ROTC also offers students the opportunity to earn two -, three-, and four -year scholarships covering full tuition and fees, book money, and a monthly allowance.

Military Science and Leadership is an elective course of study and students can participate during their freshman and sophomore years without any obligation to join the Army.
Marine and Environment-Related Programs Outstanding scholarship in marine science and oceanography at the University dates to the mid-1930s.
Over the past three decades, this strong emphasis on marine studies has extended to environmental topics, developing into an array of undergraduate programs in the natural, physical, and social sciences.
There are more than two dozen majors with a marine or environmental focus offered by URI’s colleges, including landscape architecture, physics and physical oceanography, ocean engineering, civil engineering, aquaculture and fishery technology, biological sciences, cell and molecular biology, environmental and natural resource economics, environmental science and management, geology and geological oceanography, marine affairs, marine biology, plant science, sustainable agriculture and food systems, and wildlife and conservation biology.
Several of the majors are offered jointly with the Graduate School of Oceanography.

Undergraduates are encouraged to explore opportunities at the Narragansett Bay Campus for act ive participation in the oceanographic sciences.
Juniors and seniors may take classes at the University’s Bay Campus pursuing their individual marine interests, for which they receive full academic credit.
They may also work as part of a research team in the laboratory and in the field under the direct guidance of the Graduate School of Oceanography faculty.
Center for Student Leadership Development To enhance the mission of the University of Rhode Island, the Center for Student Leadership Development aims to provide developmental opportunities for all students to become informed, inclusive, effective, and ethical leaders in the global marketplace thr ough the implementation of learner -centered academic, experiential, and co-curricular programming.
In addition, the Center engages in research, assessment, and advancement in order to positively impact the expanding field of leadership studies.
Through the College of Business, URI offers a minor in Leadership Studies that is customized for each student.
